description:
We are a team of high school students who are dedicated to computer science, engineering, space exploration, and technology solutions to real world problems. Experience in software development, Python, JavaScript, backend, data analysis and robotics. 

We aim to create something innovative and technically challenging with NASA data and resources for NASA Space Apps. We love to solve difficult problems, test new technologies and develop working prototypes out of complex ideas.
summary: POLARIS X is an interactive tool that not only tells lunar mission planners where a south-pole landing site will work, it also tells them whether it will continue to work. The lunar south pole is the area where the Sun is at the horizon, meaning that a single ridge may block a lander's access to power, or its line of sight to Earth for hours. POLARIS X calculates the line of sight for each hour, using NASA LOLA terrain data, and then recalculates it using NASA's 20 alternate terrain data maps (representing uncertainty in the elevation data). It indicates which ridges obstruct the light and when, the difference in the answer between the various terrain maps, and the minimum difference that will keep the plan on all maps. For instance, it is possible to see the Sun 100 % of the time on all 20 maps at Shackleton Rim with a 1.75 m mast. Each number is calculated from NASA/JPL data, referenced to its source, and displayed with its limitations.
details:
What it does.

The Sun will only rise and set along the horizon at the lunar south pole, and a single ridge can block a lander's power or line of sight to Earth for hours. POLARIS X allows a mission planner to select a site, a time window and a mast height, and then displays:

The skyline of the terrain around the site with the Sun and Earth tracks;

A list of hours and the visibility of the Sun, Earth and together;

When and where (“Ridge of Record”); and

Range: how the result varies across 20 NASA alternate terrain realizations (rather than one number);

Certainty Height: the lowest height of the mast at which the plan remains on all of the terrain models tested.

How it works.
Near field terrain is derived from NASA PGDA product 78 5 m LOLA DEMs (approx. ±8 km). The data for far-field terrain (up to 280 km) is derived from PGDA product 90 80 m south-polar DEM. We took 1 m steps to create a 360° horizon for each site and mast height by casting rays. The topocentric apparent Sun and Earth positions are provided hourly by JPL Horizons. We compare them with an independent NAIF SPICE (DE440) recomputation and the agreement is to about 1e-6°. We then repeat the entire computation on 20 of NASA's published terrain clones to quantify the sensitivity of the answer with respect to elevation error. Last, we check our site rankings against NASA PGDA product 69, which are 18.6 year averages of illumination and Earth-visibility maps, and find that the rank correlation of Sun and Earth is 0.72–0.93 and 0.86–0.98 respectively. The results are precomputed and then presented as versioned JSON with SHA-256 provenance, and only displayed in the web app.

Example result.
From a 1 m mast at Shackleton Rim (Site04 ROI3), the Sun can be seen 87.2–97.0 % of the time and the Sun and Earth together 62.6–74.8 % of the time, depending on the terrain map being used from the 20 terrain maps. From 1.75 m, the Sun is visible 100 % of the time on all 20. Raising the mast less than a metre makes a terrain dependent plan a strong plan.

Benefits and impact.
Typically one illumination number is reported for each site study. POLARIS X displays the range that number can assume when considering actual data uncertainty, provides the physical reason for each outage and identifies a specific engineering solution. Planners, students and the public can see the outcome and where each number has been taken from.

What makes it creative.
Instead of the question “is this site sunny?”, POLARIS X asks “does this plan survive what we don't know about the terrain?” It takes NASA's uncertainty products and turns them into a design tool, and the Certainty Height is a single actionable answer.

What we considered.
First off, scientific integrity: all numbers are derived from NASA and JPL data, and the app specifies its range. It only calculates the geometric visibility. Sun visible does not imply power and Earth visible does not imply a planned radio link. Passes on N of N terrain maps is not a calibrated probability. These are research areas at PGDA, not NASA selected landing sites. This is a research and educational prototype.
